title: WHAT IF YOU MARRIED SOMEONE YOU’RE NO LONGER ATTRACTED TO?
paragraphs:
WHAT IF YOU MARRIED SOMEONE YOU’RE NO LONGER ATTRACTED TO?
When the face you once couldn’t stop looking at becomes familiar, the feelings become complicated, and a terrifying question enters your marriage: “Did I marry the wrong person?”
There is a sentence some married Christians are terrified to say out loud.
Not because they hate their spouse.
Not because they are necessarily having an affair.
Not because they woke up wanting to destroy their family.
But because somewhere between the wedding pictures, bills, children, exhaustion, arguments, disappointments, aging bodies, unanswered expectations, and years of ordinary life…
something changed.
They look across the room at the person they once desperately wanted and quietly realize:
“I’m not attracted to you like I used to be.”
And immediately comes the guilt.
What kind of husband thinks that?
What kind of wife feels that?
Does this mean I married the wrong person?
Does this mean our marriage is dying?
Would God really expect me to spend the rest of my life with someone I no longer desire?
And then comes the question that can become far more dangerous than the feeling itself:
“What if there is someone else out there who would make me feel alive again?”
That is where this conversation becomes serious.
Because losing a feeling is one thing.
Building a theology that gives you permission to betray your covenant because of that feeling is another.
You need to hear this before we go any further:
Temptation is not the same thing as surrender.
An unwanted thought is not the same thing as an affair.
Recognizing that another human being is attractive is not identical to deliberately feeding lust.
And experiencing a season in which attraction toward your spouse has weakened does not automatically mean your marriage was a mistake.
But what you do with that weakness matters enormously.
Jesus takes the inner life seriously.

In Matthew 5:28, He speaks about looking at another person “with lustful intent.” The Greek uses the expression πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν — pros to epithymēsai autēn — pointing beyond merely possessing functioning eyes toward a look joined to covetous desire.
Jesus goes after the heart.
Because adultery rarely begins in a hotel room.
Sometimes it begins in imagination.
Comparison.
A private message.
A conversation you know you would not want your spouse reading.
A fantasy you repeatedly feed.
A coworker whose attention feels intoxicating because you have not felt noticed at home in years.

A person on a screen whose body has never aged beside you, never been sick beside you, never argued over money with you, never raised children with you, never carried the accumulated weight of actual life with you.
Fantasy has an enormous advantage over covenant:
Fantasy never has to become ordinary.
Your spouse does.
That may be one of the most important things you ever understand about attraction.
The stranger can remain mysterious.
The person online can remain carefully presented.
The old flame can remain preserved in memory.
The attractive coworker can remain associated with laughter, competence, perfume, confidence, or an hour without screaming children.
But your spouse?
You have seen them exhausted.
You have smelled their morning breath.
You know their insecurities.
You remember their worst arguments.
You know which drawer they never close.
You know their weaknesses.
You have watched their body change.
And they have watched yours change too.
Familiarity removes illusion.
But familiarity can also reveal something infinitely deeper than illusion:
covenant.
The Bible never commands married people to pretend physical attraction does not matter.
Scripture is remarkably unembarrassed about marital desire.
Read Song of Songs.

The husband and wife delight in one another. They notice beauty. They long for closeness. Biblical marriage is not supposed to be a cold business arrangement in which two people merely tolerate one another until death.
Paul likewise refuses to treat marital intimacy as insignificant.
In 1 Corinthians 7:3, he writes:
The Greek speaks of what is owed within the marital relationship, and the surrounding verses explicitly address sexual intimacy.
So no—Christianity does not require you to become a disembodied creature who feels nothing.
Attraction matters.
Sexual intimacy matters.
Tenderness matters.
Being wanted matters.
Being touched matters.
Being seen matters.
And if those things have disappeared from your marriage, dismissing the pain with “just pray harder” may leave wounds untreated.
But here is where our culture often deceives us.
Something can matter without becoming your master.
Attraction is a beautiful servant.
It is a terrible god.
Because if attraction becomes the foundation of your covenant, what happens when bodies change?
Pregnancy changes bodies.
Illness changes bodies.
Medication can change bodies.
Hormones change bodies.
Depression and grief can affect desire.
Stress can affect desire.
Age changes bodies.
Disability can change bodies.
Menopause changes bodies.
Hair disappears.
Skin loosens.
Scars appear.
Strength fades.
Sexual functioning can change.
And eventually every married couple who remains alive long enough discovers something Instagram cannot sell:
You did not marry a photograph.
You married a person.
This is where Christian marriage becomes radically different from the disposable relationships our culture often celebrates.
Your spouse was never promised permanent youth.
Neither were you.

Imagine a husband looking at the woman who carried his children, survived sleepless nights, prayed beside him when money disappeared, held his hand at funerals, forgave failures nobody else knows about, and remained when life became ugly…
then deciding she has become less worthy of his devotion because gravity touched her body.
Imagine a wife measuring the husband who has worked, failed, repented, aged, struggled, protected, cried, prayed, and remained beside her against the carefully edited appearance of another man.
Something has gone terribly wrong when we can remember somebody’s changing waistline more easily than their sacrifices.
But there is another side to this conversation.
Sometimes “I’m not attracted to my spouse anymore” is not really about appearance.
Sometimes it means:
“I’m still hurt.”
“I don’t feel emotionally safe.”
“We stopped talking.”
“I feel invisible.”
“I’m carrying resentment.”
“He stopped pursuing me.”
“She constantly rejects me.”
“We have become roommates.”
“Pornography has distorted what turns me on.”
“I compare my spouse with people online.”
“We stopped touching unless sex was expected.”
“I have been emotionally neglected.”
“We never repaired what happened three years ago.”
“I don’t know this person anymore.”
And sometimes physical attraction is blamed for a wound that actually lives somewhere much deeper.
A marriage can lose erotic warmth because affection died slowly under a thousand unresolved injuries.
That does not mean every attraction problem is psychological or spiritual. Human sexuality is complex, and medical, hormonal, relational, psychological, and situational factors can all matter.
But before declaring, “I married the wrong person,” ask a more frightening question:
“What happened between us?”
And then ask another:
“What happened inside me?”
Because sometimes the person beside you did change.
And sometimes you did.
Sometimes both did.
Maybe pornography trained your eyes to expect novelty.
Maybe social media trained you to compare an ordinary spouse against extraordinary presentation.
Maybe resentment made tenderness difficult.
Maybe you stopped dating each other after marriage.
Maybe neither of you takes care of yourselves anymore—not because either spouse owes the other a flawless body, but because discouragement swallowed your shared life.
Maybe years of criticism turned desire into defensiveness.
Maybe one of you stopped listening.
Maybe sex became transactional.
Maybe parenthood consumed husbandhood and wifehood.
Maybe you started noticing everything your spouse lacks while forgetting everything they have faithfully given.
And maybe there is another person.
That possibility needs to be confronted without euphemism.
If another person has suddenly made your spouse look dull, be very careful.
Novelty is powerful.
Forbidden attention can be intoxicating.
You may think you have discovered your “soulmate” when what you have actually discovered is dopamine without responsibility.
The other person does not currently carry the weight your spouse carries.
You are comparing somebody’s highlight reel with your spouse’s behind-the-scenes footage.
You are comparing possibility with history.
Mystery with familiarity.
Fantasy with flesh.
And fantasy almost always wins when the competition is rigged.
Jesus does not invite us to nurture that fantasy.
He calls us toward purity of heart.
This is where another Greek word becomes important.
When Paul tells husbands in Ephesians 5:25 to love their wives, the word is ἀγαπᾶτε — agapate, from agapaō.
“Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the church and gave Himself for her.”
Notice the standard.
Not:
Love her as long as butterflies remain.
Not:
Love her until someone prettier arrives.
Not:
Love her while she maintains the body she had at twenty-five.
Christ loved the Church and “gave Himself.”
Christian love therefore cannot be reduced to romantic chemistry.
It moves toward self-giving.
That does not mean attraction is irrelevant.
It means attraction does not sit on the throne.
Jesus does.
And this may hurt:
Your spouse was never created to keep you perpetually stimulated.
They were not placed on earth to satisfy every fantasy.
Marriage cannot carry the weight of being your god.
Only Christ can.

When we expect a spouse to continually make us feel young, desirable, fascinated, sexually electrified, emotionally fulfilled, spiritually complete, and permanently happy, we demand from a human being something no human being can sustain.
Then when they inevitably fail, we call the covenant defective.
Perhaps the covenant is not always the problem.
Perhaps sometimes our expectations need to die.
And strangely, that death can become the birthplace of a deeper love.
There is a Hebrew word Scripture uses for covenant faithfulness and steadfast love: חֶסֶד — ḥesed.
Its range of meaning is rich and cannot be collapsed into one English word, but it regularly carries ideas such as steadfast love, loyal love, mercy, kindness, and covenant faithfulness.
That kind of love has weight.
It remains meaningful when emotion fluctuates.

It does not mean enduring abuse without seeking safety. Scripture must never be weaponized to trap someone in immediate danger, excuse violence, or silence serious wrongdoing. If abuse, coercion, threats, or danger are present, seeking safety and qualified help is not a betrayal of biblical faithfulness.
But in an ordinary marriage facing fading attraction, disappointment, familiarity, or relational distance, covenant asks a different question from consumer culture.
Consumer culture asks:
“Am I still getting what I want?”
Covenant asks:
“How can we become faithful again?”
That word we matters.
A healthy marriage should not become one spouse desperately carrying the entire relationship while the other refuses responsibility.
Both spouses may need humility.
Both may need repentance.
Both may need uncomfortable conversations.
Both may need to relearn tenderness.
Both may need to ask forgiveness.
Both may need to become curious about one another again.
Both may need to shut certain screens off.
Both may need to stop comparing.
Both may need to rebuild trust.
Both may need to pursue physical and emotional health—not to earn love, but because caring for ourselves and one another can be an expression of stewardship.
Maybe you need to date your spouse again.
Not the imaginary version you married.
The person standing before you now.
Learn them again.
Ask what hurts.
Ask what they miss.
Ask when they stopped feeling wanted.
Ask what makes them feel safe.
Ask what makes them feel cherished.
Ask what you stopped doing.
Then have enough humility to hear an answer you may not like.
Perhaps attraction does not always need to be “found.”
Sometimes it needs to be cultivated.
Think about a garden.
Nobody stands over neglected soil after seven years and screams:
“Why aren't there flowers?”
You water it.
You remove weeds.
You expose what is choking the roots.
You nourish what remains alive.
You protect what is tender.
You wait.
You work.
You pray.
And sometimes something you assumed was dead begins pushing through the soil.
This is not a promise that every marriage will suddenly become passionate if you follow the correct formula.
The Bible does not give us permission to manufacture guarantees God never gave.
But reconciliation, repentance, renewed affection, forgiveness, and restored intimacy are real possibilities.
And Jesus Christ specializes in resurrection.
That is the center of this entire conversation.
Not your attractiveness.
Not your spouse’s attractiveness.
Not sexual technique.
Not romantic nostalgia.
Jesus.
Because the Gospel tells the story of a Bridegroom whose love is radically unlike our shallow measurements of worth.
Christ did not wait until His Bride was impressive enough to deserve Him.
Romans 5:8 says:
“God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were sinners.
Not after we became beautiful enough.
Not after we fixed ourselves.
Not after we became convenient to love.
Christ moved toward undeserving sinners in sacrificial grace.
That does not make every detail of Christ's relationship with His Church interchangeable with human marriage.
But it gives Christian spouses a breathtaking picture of love:
Grace moves toward the undeserving.
Grace tells the truth.
Grace does not call sin righteousness.
Grace forgives the repentant.
Grace seeks restoration.
Grace remembers covenant.
And grace can rewrite stories that look finished.
Maybe your marriage has become a scandal nobody knows about.
Maybe you sleep inches apart but feel miles away.
Maybe everybody sees the anniversary photos and assumes you are happy.
Maybe you kissed your spouse goodbye this morning while secretly wondering whether you still love them.
Maybe another person has entered your imagination.
Maybe pornography has quietly colonized your desires.
Maybe your spouse's rejection has crushed your confidence.
Maybe you feel ashamed because you desperately want to want them again…
but you don't know how.
Bring that truth to Jesus.
Not the polished version.
The ugly version.
The version you are embarrassed to pray.
“Jesus, my heart is wandering.”
“Jesus, I have compared my spouse.”
“Jesus, I have neglected them.”
“Jesus, I am wounded.”
“Jesus, I have entertained thoughts I should have rejected.”
“Jesus, I don't know how to rebuild this.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
Repentance is not humiliation for humiliation's sake.
Repentance is turning.
The Greek New Testament uses μετάνοια — metanoia — for repentance, carrying the sense of a changed mind, a turning of one's inner orientation that bears fruit in life.
Turn toward Christ.
Then, where it is wise and safe, turn toward your spouse.
You may need a serious conversation.
You may need a trustworthy pastor.
You may need a qualified Christian marriage counselor or other competent professional.
You may need medical evaluation if desire changed suddenly or significantly.
You may need to confess pornography.
You may need to establish boundaries with another person before emotional infidelity becomes physical adultery.
You may need to delete messages.
You may need to stop protecting a fantasy that is poisoning your covenant.
You may need to apologize without saying “but.”
And you may need to remember something beautiful:
The person beside you is more than the body you are evaluating.
That is an image-bearer of God.
A soul.
A person Jesus died to redeem.
A person with fears you may have forgotten.
A person who may also be wondering whether you still see them.
Maybe tonight, instead of asking:
“Why don't you look like you used to?”
ask:
“When did I stop looking at you with tenderness?”
Instead of asking:
“Could I find someone more attractive?”
ask:
“What would happen if I invested that energy into becoming intimate with my spouse again?”
Instead of scrolling through bodies engineered to awaken dissatisfaction, put the phone down.
Look across the room.
There is a human being there.
Not an algorithm.
Not pornography.
Not a fantasy.
Not a profile picture.
A human being.
Perhaps wounded.
Perhaps imperfect.
Perhaps aging.
Perhaps difficult.
Perhaps lonely.
Perhaps waiting to know whether the person who once promised “for better or worse” still means it when “worse” becomes ordinary Tuesday night.
And maybe your spouse needs to hear something they have not heard from you in a painfully long time:
“I still choose us.”
Not because feelings never matter.
But because feelings were never meant to be your lord.
Jesus is.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, don't turn the conviction into shame and disappear.
Bring it into the light.

And if sharing those words publicly would put you in danger or expose private circumstances that should remain confidential, you do not owe the internet your private pain. Bring it to God and to trustworthy people who can actually walk beside you.
But don't keep this article only for yourself.
Someone on your Facebook friends list may be sitting beside their spouse tonight asking the exact question they are ashamed to say aloud.
Not because clicking “Share” earns favor with God. It does not.

But if this ministry is helping people encounter biblical truth, supporting and sharing Gospel-centered work can become one voluntary way of participating in getting that truth in front of someone who needs it.
Send it privately to someone who needs grace more than public attention.
It cannot purchase blessing.
It cannot prove your faith.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.

But financially supporting Gospel-centered ministry can be one practical expression of generosity when it is given freely, wisely, and cheerfully. Your support helps us keep creating and sharing Christ-centered resources intended to call people toward repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, and transformation through the Gospel.
Come back to Jesus.
If you have sinned, repent.
If you have wandered, return.
If you have wounded your spouse, seek forgiveness.
If you have been wounded, seek wise help and bring the wound into the light.
If your marriage is dry, don't immediately assume dry means dead.
If attraction has faded, don't automatically translate that feeling into a verdict that God gave you the wrong person.
You may be staring at the end of one kind of love…
only to discover that Christ is teaching you a deeper one.
Because someday, if God gives you enough years together, neither of you will look like the people standing in your wedding photographs.
Your hands may shake.
Your hair may thin.
Your faces may carry lines.
Your bodies may become fragile.
And perhaps one day one of you will sit beside a hospital bed holding the hand of the person who no longer resembles the young man or woman you married.
At that moment, beauty may look entirely different.
Beauty may be fifty years of forgiveness.
Beauty may be staying.
Beauty may be repentance after failure.
Beauty may be learning how to laugh again after almost losing everything.
Beauty may be wrinkled hands still reaching for each other.
Beauty may be two sinners who discovered that marriage was never about finding somebody perfect enough to worship.
It was about two imperfect people continually needing the perfect Savior.
And maybe that is the answer to the question you were afraid to ask.
“What if I married someone I'm no longer attracted to?”
Then don't worship attraction.
Tell the truth.
Guard your heart.
Deal honestly with what has damaged desire.
Seek wise help.
Reject fantasy.
Pursue intimacy.
Practice tenderness.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where biblical forgiveness is possible.
Remember your covenant.
And above everything else…
look to Christ.
Because the deepest hope for your marriage is not that your spouse somehow becomes twenty-five again.
It is that both of you become more like Jesus.

You may no longer recognize the people in your wedding photograph—but by the grace of Christ, you may someday discover that what grew between you became more beautiful than what first drew you together.
